summary.text: Lucas-type binomial congruences pair the two halves of each defining sum to show that both moment sequences vanish modulo \(p\) at \(p+r\) for \(0\le r<p-1\); at the boundary they give \(a(p-1)=1\) and \(c(p-1)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), with all but the middle term of the latter sum killed by divisibility of a central binomial coefficient by \(p\). Thus both Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\), and reversing the columns reduces their determinants to the reversal sign \((-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\) times the anti-diagonal product, yielding the first sign and cancellation to \(1\) in the second case.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                         \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and perform all computations below in the field \(\mathbf F_p\), unless an integer identity is explicitly indicated. We prove the two determinant congruences by showing that the relevant Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\), and then evaluating their anti-diagonals.

We first record the binomial congruences that will be used.

By Lucas's theorem, for all nonnegative integers \(N,K\),
\[
 \binom NK\equiv
 \binom{N\bmod p}{K\bmod p}
 \binom{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{\lfloor K/p\rfloor}\pmod p,
\]
with the same statement applied recursively if the quotients still have more than one base-\(p\) digit. In particular, if \(0\le r<p\) and \(0\le k<2p\), then
\[
\boxed{\binom{p+r}{k}\equiv \binom r{k\bmod p}\pmod p.}\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the leading base-\(p\) digit of \(p+r\) is \(1\), while \(\lfloor k/p\rfloor\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), and both \(\binom10\) and \(\binom11\) equal \(1\).

We shall also need
\[
\boxed{\binom{2(p+k)}{p+k}\equiv 2\binom{2k}{k}\pmod p}
\qquad(0\le k<p).\tag{2}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2k<p\), Lucas's theorem applied to numerator \(2p+2k\) and denominator \(p+k\) gives
\[
 \binom{2p+2k}{p+k}\equiv \binom21\binom{2k}{k}
 =2\binom{2k}{k}.
\]
If \(2k\ge p\), write \(2k=p+s\), where \(s=2k-p<k\). The units digit in the base-\(p\) expansion of the numerator \(2k\) is \(s\), whereas the units digit of \(k\) is \(k\). Hence Lucas's theorem gives
\( inom{2k}{k}\equiv0\), since \(\binom sk=0\). The same units digits \(s\) and \(k\) occur for the numerator \(2p+2k\) and denominator \(p+k\), so the left side of (2) is also zero. Thus (2) holds in both cases.

The same argument gives the useful vanishing criterion
\[
\boxed{0\le k<p,\quad 2k\ge p
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \binom{2k}{k}\equiv0\pmod p.}\tag{3}
\]

Finally, for \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\boxed{\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\pmod p.}\tag{4}
\]
For example, this follows directly from
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}= rac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
 \equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k\pmod p.
\]
The denominator is invertible because \(k<p\).

We next establish the crucial vanishing of the sequence values whose indices lie between \(p\) and \(2p-2\).

### 1. Vanishing of \(a(p+r)\)

Let \(0\le r<p-1\). Split the defining sum at \(p\):
\[
a(p+r)=
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4
 +\sum_{k=p}^{p+r}(-1)^k\binom{p+r}{k}^4.
\]
For \(0\le k<p\), congruence (1) gives
\( inom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk\). Terms with \(k>r\) vanish, so the first sum is
\[
 S:=\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^k\binom rk^4.
\]
In the second sum put \(k=p+t\), where \(0\le t\le r\). Again by (1),
\[
 \binom{p+r}{p+t}\equiv\binom rt.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \((-1)^p=-1\), and hence
\[
 (-1)^{p+t}=-(-1)^t.
\]
The second sum is therefore \(-S\). Consequently
\[
\boxed{a(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(0\le r<p-1).}\tag{5}
\]

### 2. Vanishing of \(c(p+r)\)

Again let \(0\le r<p-1\), and split the defining sum for \(c(p+r)\) into the ranges \(0\le k<p\) and \(p\le k\le p+r\).

Consider first \(0\le k<p\). By (1),
\( inom{p+r}{k}\equiv\binom rk\), so terms with \(k>r\) vanish. If \(k\le r\), then
\[
p+r-k=p+(r-k),
\]
and (2), applied with \(r-k<p\), gives
\[
 \binom{2(p+r-k)}{p+r-k}
 \equiv2\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}.
\]
Thus the first block of the sum is congruent to
\[
2T,
\quad\text{where}\quad
T=\sum_{k=0}^{r}(-1)^k\binom rk^2
       \binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(r-k)}{r-k}.
\]

In the second block write \(k=p+t\), with \(0\le t\le r\). We then have
\[
 \binom{p+r}{p+t}\equiv\binom rt,
 \qquad p+r-(p+t)=r-t,
\]
and by (2),
\[
 \binom{2(p+t)}{p+t}\equiv2\binom{2t}{t}.
\]
Also \((-1)^{p+t}=-(-1)^t\). Hence the second block is congruent to \(-2T\). It follows that
\[
\boxed{c(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad(0\le r<p-1).}\tag{6}
\]

We now calculate the values on the future anti-diagonal, namely the values at \(p-1\).

### 3. The value of \(a(p-1)\)

By (4),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4\\
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, the alternating sum of these \(p\) terms is \(1\). Thus
\[
\boxed{a(p-1)\equiv1\pmod p.}\tag{7}
\]

### 4. The value of \(c(p-1)\)

Write
\[
p=2m+1,
\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
We claim that, modulo \(p\), every term in the defining sum for \(c(p-1)\) vanishes except the term with \(k=m\).

Indeed, if \(k<m\), put \(\ell=p-1-k=2m-k\). Then \(0\le\ell<p\) and
\[
2\ell=2(p-1-k)\ge p.
\]
Thus (3) shows
\( inom{2\ell}{\ell}\equiv0\), which kills the final central-binomial factor of that summand. If \(k>m\), then \(2k\ge p\), so (3) instead gives \(\binom{2k}{k}\equiv0\). These are all the terms other than \(k=m\).

For \(k=m\), one has \(p-1-m=m\), so the surviving term equals
\[
 (-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^2\binom{2m}{m}^2.
\]
Since \(2m=p-1\), congruence (4) says both
\[
 \binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m,
 \qquad
 \binom{2m}{m}\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
Their squares are \(1\), and hence
\[
\boxed{c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m
      =(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.}\tag{8}
\]

We next give the determinant reduction that will be used for both matrices.

### 5. Determinant of an anti-triangular matrix

Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) be a matrix over a commutative ring such that
\[
M_{ij}=0\qquad\text{whenever }i+j>p-1.
\]
In the permutation expansion
\[
\det M=\sum_{\sigma\in S_p}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
                     \prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,\sigma(i)},
\]
a nonzero product can occur only if
\[
i+\sigma(i)\le p-1\qquad\text{for every }i.
\]
But summing these inequalities gives equality term by term. More explicitly,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\bigl((p-1)-i-\sigma(i)\bigr)=0,
\]
because
\[
\sum_i i=\sum_i\sigma(i)=\frac{p(p-1)}2.
\]
Each summand is a nonnegative integer, so every summand is zero. Therefore
\[
\sigma(i)=p-1-i
\]
for every \(i\). Thus only the reversal permutation \(\rho(i)=p-1-i\) survives, and
\[
\boxed{\det M=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)
              \prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,p-1-i}.}\tag{9}
\]
The reversal has one inversion for every pair of distinct indices in increasing order, hence
\[
\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^{\binom p2}
=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.\tag{10}
\]

### 6. The determinant formed from \(a\)

Let
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Reduce its entries modulo \(p\). If \(i+j>p-1\), then, because \(i,j<p\),
\[
p\le i+j\le2p-2.
\]
We may therefore write
\[
i+j=p+r,
\qquad 0\le r\le p-2,

a condition equivalent to \(0\le r<p-1\). By (5),
\[
a(i+j)=a(p+r)\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(A\) is anti-triangular modulo \(p\). Every entry on its anti-diagonal has index
\(i+(p-1-i)=p-1\), and by (7) each such entry is \(1\). Formula (9) now gives
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm=(2m+1)m\equiv m\pmod2.
\]
Powers of \(-1\) depend only on the parity of the exponent, so
\[
(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}=(-1)^m=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}
       \equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.}
\]

### 7. The determinant formed from \(c\)

Let
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Exactly the same index argument, now using (6), shows that
\[
c(i+j)\equiv0\pmod p\qquad\text{if }i+j>p-1.
\]
Hence \(C\) is also anti-triangular modulo \(p\). By (8), all of its \(p\) anti-diagonal entries equal \((-1)^m\), where \(m=(p-1)/2\). Their product is
\[
\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}c(p-1)
\equiv\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p=(-1)^{mp}
=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Combining this with (9) and (10),
\[
\det C\equiv
(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}
=(-1)^{p(p-1)}=1\pmod p,
\]
since \(p(p-1)\) is even. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.}
\]

Both asserted congruences follow.
